features.name: Landing_Page
features.purpose: Serves as the entry point to BWS4, explaining what the project is, stating plainly that BWS4 and every example inside it were built with Spec4, and presenting the roster of example apps so a visitor can choose one to explore.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens BWS4, or returns to the entry point from anywhere in the app via the persistent navigation.

inputs.name: project introduction content
inputs.description: Short explanation of BWS4's purpose, its relationship to Spec4, and how to use the gallery.

inputs.name: example app roster
inputs.description: For each available example app: its display name, the agentic pattern it illustrates, and a one-line summary of what a visitor will see.

inputs.name: visitor selection
inputs.description: The example app the visitor chooses to open.

outputs.primary: An introductory overview plus a browsable list of example apps, and navigation into the chosen example app.
outputs.format: On-screen page content with navigation available from every part of the app
outputs.schema_notes: Each roster entry carries name, pattern label, and short summary; entries are ordered so simpler patterns appear before more complex ones.

success_criteria: A first-time visitor can state, after reading the entry page, what BWS4 is and that it was built with Spec4
Every example app currently available in BWS4 appears exactly once in the roster and in the persistent navigation
Selecting any roster entry opens that example app, and the visitor can return to the entry point from any example app
The roster and navigation stay consistent with each other at all times

failure_modes.mode: An example app exists but is missing from the roster or navigation, so visitors never find it
failure_modes.mitigation: The roster and navigation are both drawn from one shared description of available examples, so an example cannot appear in one place and not the other

failure_modes.mode: Introduction is too abstract, leaving evaluators unsure what they are looking at
failure_modes.mitigation: Lead with a plain-language statement of purpose and the Spec4 provenance, and keep each roster summary to one concrete sentence

failure_modes.mode: A listed example app is temporarily unavailable and the visitor hits a dead end
failure_modes.mitigation: Unavailable examples are shown with a clear explanatory note instead of silently failing when opened

features.name: RAG_Example_App
features.purpose: Demonstrates the retrieval-augmented generation pattern: a visitor's question is answered by first finding the most relevant passages in a small public collection and then having a model answer using only those passages, with the retrieved evidence shown alongside the answer.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the RAG example from the entry point or navigation and submits a question or selects a preset question.

inputs.name: visitor question
inputs.description: The question to be answered from the curated collection.

inputs.name: preset question choice
inputs.description: A curated question chosen instead of typing one, illustrating good and poor retrieval cases.

inputs.name: curated collection
inputs.description: A small, publicly available body of text passages that forms the app's knowledge scope.

outputs.primary: An answer grounded in retrieved passages, shown together with the passages that were retrieved and the similarity ordering that selected them.
outputs.format: On-screen answer plus visible retrieved evidence and a short educational overview of the pattern
outputs.schema_notes: Each retrieved passage shows its source document, its excerpt, and its relative relevance; the answer indicates which passages it drew on.

success_criteria: A visitor can see, for any question, which passages were retrieved and how the answer used them
Questions inside the collection's scope produce answers traceable to the shown passages
Questions outside the collection's scope produce an honest 'not covered by this collection' response rather than an invented answer
A visitor can articulate afterwards why retrieval was performed before generation
The example runs entirely on the shared framework capabilities

failure_modes.mode: Retrieved passages are irrelevant, producing a confidently wrong answer
failure_modes.mitigation: Always display the retrieved passages so the visitor can see the cause, and instruct the answering step to decline when the passages do not contain the answer

failure_modes.mode: The model answers from general knowledge, ignoring the retrieved passages, hiding the pattern
failure_modes.mitigation: Require the answer to reference the passages it used, and flag answers that cite none

failure_modes.mode: The collection is too large or too slow to search, making the demo sluggish
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep the collection deliberately small and prepare its comparable representations ahead of a visitor's first question

failure_modes.mode: Model capacity is exhausted mid-question
failure_modes.mitigation: Show the retrieved passages that were obtained plus a clear message about which usage cap was reached

features.name: Shared_Framework_Services
features.purpose: Provides the common capabilities every example app relies on — text generation from a language model, turning text into comparable numeric representations, web search, and keeping small amounts of app data — so each example demonstrates a pattern rather than re-inventing infrastructure.

invocation.trigger: An example app requests one of the shared capabilities during a run.

inputs.name: generation request
inputs.description: The instruction or conversation an example app wants a language model to respond to, optionally with a description of the shape the answer should take.

inputs.name: text to represent numerically
inputs.description: Items an example app wants converted into comparable numeric representations for similarity or clustering purposes.

inputs.name: search request
inputs.description: A query an example app wants answered from public web content.

inputs.name: data record request
inputs.description: Small pieces of app data an example app wants to keep or retrieve.

inputs.name: usage context
inputs.description: Which example app and which visitor visit a request belongs to, so usage limits can be applied.

outputs.primary: Model-generated text or structured answers, numeric text representations, web search results, retrieved app data, and clear signals when a usage limit has been reached.
outputs.format: Uniform results and uniform failure signals returned to the calling example app
outputs.schema_notes: Every result carries either the requested content or an explicit reason for failure (limit reached, capability unavailable, request rejected); usage accounting distinguishes per-example limits from the shared hourly and daily framework caps.

success_criteria: Every example app obtains generation, numeric text representation, search, and small-data capabilities without introducing its own equivalents
Generation requests succeed at no cost to visitors under normal conditions
When a usage cap is reached, calling apps receive an unambiguous signal identifying which cap was hit rather than an opaque error
Shared hourly and daily usage caps are never exceeded, regardless of visitor traffic
A capability outage in one shared service leaves other example apps that do not use it fully functional

failure_modes.mode: Language model capacity is unavailable or refuses a request
failure_modes.mitigation: Return a clear, distinguishable signal so example apps can explain the situation to the visitor, and allow an alternative model of equivalent capability to serve the request

failure_modes.mode: Web search returns nothing useful or is unreachable
failure_modes.mitigation: Report the empty or failed result explicitly so calling apps can continue candidly rather than fabricating observations

failure_modes.mode: A single visitor or example consumes a disproportionate share of daily model capacity
failure_modes.mitigation: Enforce per-example and per-visit limits alongside shared hourly and daily caps, and account for every request before it is issued

failure_modes.mode: Numeric text representations differ between calls, making comparisons inconsistent
failure_modes.mitigation: Guarantee that identical text always yields identical representations for the lifetime of a comparison set

failure_modes.mode: Generation latency makes examples feel broken
failure_modes.mitigation: Surface progress signals to calling apps as soon as work starts and expose partial results where the pattern allows

features.name: Tool_Use_Integration
features.purpose: Gives example apps that need external facts a single shared way to search the public web and receive result snippets, so tool use is demonstrated consistently and accounted for centrally.

invocation.trigger: An example app decides, during a run, that it needs external information and issues a search request.

inputs.name: search query
inputs.description: The exact query the requesting model or app wants searched.

inputs.name: result count preference
inputs.description: How many result snippets are wanted, within a small ceiling.

inputs.name: usage context
inputs.description: Which example app and visit the search belongs to, for limit accounting.

outputs.primary: A small ordered set of web result snippets with their titles and source references, or an explicit empty/failed result.
outputs.format: Uniform search result set returned to the calling example app and displayable to the visitor
outputs.schema_notes: Each result carries a title, a short excerpt, and a citable source reference; the set records the exact query issued so it can be shown in traces.

success_criteria: Any example app needing external facts can search without introducing its own search capability
The exact query issued is always available for display alongside its results, so traces are honest
Results are relevant enough that a model can answer time-variable questions correctly
Search requests count toward the shared usage accounting
An unsuccessful or empty search is reported as such and never silently presented as an observation

failure_modes.mode: Search returns irrelevant or low-quality snippets, derailing a run
failure_modes.mitigation: Return several ranked snippets rather than one, and pass them through verbatim so the model and the visitor can judge relevance

failure_modes.mode: Search capability is unreachable or rate limited
failure_modes.mitigation: Report the failure distinctly so calling apps can degrade candidly and continue or stop with an explanation

failure_modes.mode: Excessive searching in one run exhausts the shared allowance for other visitors
failure_modes.mitigation: Cap searches per run and per visit and account for every search centrally before it is issued

failure_modes.mode: Snippets are too short to support multi-hop reasoning
failure_modes.mitigation: Return excerpts long enough to carry the answering fact, and allow a follow-up query on the same topic

features.name: Embeddings_Example_App
features.purpose: Makes the embeddings pattern visible: a curated mix of short category words and full sentences is turned into comparable numeric representations, projected onto a two-dimensional plot, and shown clustering by meaning, with the visitor able to add their own text and see where it lands.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the Embeddings example from the entry point or navigation; the plot is produced on arrival, and re-produced whenever the visitor adds custom text.

inputs.name: curated text examples
inputs.description: Pre-configured short words and phrases grouped into recognisable categories such as animals, emotions and technical terms, plus a set of full sentences.

inputs.name: custom visitor text
inputs.description: One or more free-form phrases or sentences the visitor wants placed on the same plot.

outputs.primary: A two-dimensional plot of all texts positioned by semantic similarity, with curated points grouped visibly by category and any visitor-supplied points rendered distinctly.
outputs.format: Interactive plot with point labels, plus a short educational overview of the embeddings pattern
outputs.schema_notes: Every point carries its original text, its category (or 'your text'), and its plotted position; visitor points are visually distinguished from curated ones.

success_criteria: Semantically related curated texts appear near one another and unrelated ones appear apart, clearly enough for a visitor to see clustering without explanation
Adding custom text results in a single recalculated plot containing both curated and custom points, with the custom points immediately identifiable
The visitor can read the text behind any point on the plot
The example produces its representations from the framework's existing shared capability, with no separate model of its own
The overview leaves a visitor able to explain what an embedding is and what proximity on the plot means

failure_modes.mode: The projection to two dimensions shows no visible clustering, defeating the lesson
failure_modes.mitigation: Curate categories that are strongly distinct from one another and verify visible separation before the example is offered

failure_modes.mode: Adding custom text rearranges the plot so much that the visitor loses their bearings
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep category grouping and labelling stable across recalculations and highlight the newly added points

failure_modes.mode: Very long or empty custom input produces a meaningless point
failure_modes.mitigation: Accept only non-empty text within a stated length, explaining the limit plainly when it is exceeded

failure_modes.mode: Recalculation after custom input takes long enough to feel broken
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep the curated set small, show that work is in progress, and complete recalculation within a couple of seconds

features.name: Single_Call_Example_App
features.purpose: Demonstrates the simplest agentic pattern — one request to a language model producing one response, with no retrieval, no tools and no chaining — and shows the difference between asking for plain prose and asking for an answer in a caller-specified shape.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the Single Call example, supplies or selects a prompt, and starts the run.

inputs.name: visitor prompt
inputs.description: A free-form instruction for the model.

inputs.name: preset prompt choice
inputs.description: One of a curated set of illustrative tasks such as summarising, classifying or extracting.

inputs.name: response mode
inputs.description: Whether the visitor wants a plain-prose response or a response conforming to a requested shape.

outputs.primary: The model's single response, plus — in shaped mode — the exact request that described the desired shape and the shaped answer that came back.
outputs.format: On-screen request and response display, with a short educational overview of the single-call pattern and when it suits a problem
outputs.schema_notes: In plain mode, prose only. In shaped mode, both the shape description sent and the conforming answer received are displayed, with any deviation from the requested shape flagged.

success_criteria: Exactly one model request is made per run, and the visitor can see that only one occurred
Preset prompts each produce a recognisably appropriate result, illustrating summarise, classify and extract tasks
In shaped mode the visitor sees both what was asked for and what came back, and the returned answer matches the requested shape
Switching modes with the same prompt visibly changes the form but not the substance of the answer
The example uses only the framework's shared generation capability

failure_modes.mode: The model's shaped answer does not conform to the requested shape
failure_modes.mitigation: Detect non-conformance, show the raw answer, and explain plainly that shaped output is requested rather than guaranteed — itself a teaching point

failure_modes.mode: A visitor submits an empty or extremely long prompt
failure_modes.mitigation: Require non-empty input within a stated length and explain the limit clearly

failure_modes.mode: A visitor submits abusive or unsafe input
failure_modes.mitigation: Pass through the model's refusal candidly and explain that refusal is a legitimate single-call outcome

failure_modes.mode: Model capacity is exhausted
failure_modes.mitigation: State which usage cap was reached and leave the submitted prompt on screen

features.name: Chained_Calls_Example_App
features.purpose: Demonstrates the chained-calls pattern by running exactly two model calls where the first call's output becomes the second call's input, showing both the intermediate and final results so the hand-off is visible.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the Chained Calls example, enters or selects an initial request, and starts the run.

inputs.name: initial request
inputs.description: The visitor's starting request, handled by the first stage in the chain.

inputs.name: preset request choice
inputs.description: A curated starting request that shows the chain to good effect.

outputs.primary: The intermediate result from the first stage and the final result from the second stage, both labelled with that stage's stated role.
outputs.format: Sequential on-screen stage results, with a short educational overview of the chained-calls pattern
outputs.schema_notes: Each stage shows its declared role, its input, and its output; the display makes explicit that the second stage's input is the first stage's output.

success_criteria: Each stage's role is stated before the run so the visitor knows what to expect
Both the intermediate and final results are shown, and the visitor can see that the second stage consumed the first stage's output
Exactly two model calls occur per run
The page states plainly that the two-call limit conserves model capacity for this demo and that the pattern itself supports any number of chained calls
The final result is visibly better suited to the visitor's request than the intermediate result alone

failure_modes.mode: The first stage produces a weak or off-topic output, degrading the final result
failure_modes.mitigation: Show the intermediate output so the cause is visible, and offer presets known to chain well

failure_modes.mode: The second stage ignores the first stage's output, hiding the pattern
failure_modes.mitigation: Give each stage a distinct, narrow role and display both inputs and outputs so any disconnect is apparent

failure_modes.mode: The run fails after the first call, leaving the visitor with half a result
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep the intermediate result on screen and explain that the second stage did not complete and why

failure_modes.mode: Visitors mistake the two-call limit for a limitation of the pattern
failure_modes.mitigation: State the quota rationale prominently next to the run itself, not only in the overview

features.name: Planning_Agent_Example_App
features.purpose: Demonstrates the plan-first planning-agent pattern through a one-day trip planner: a planner call decomposes the visitor's goal into a small set of discrete steps, the plan is shown for review before anything runs, and separate executor calls then carry out the steps — research steps using shared web search plus a final synthesis into an itinerary.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the Planning Agent example and submits a city and interests, which produces a plan; the visitor then advances the run to execute the plan's steps in order.

inputs.name: city
inputs.description: The destination the itinerary should cover.

inputs.name: interests
inputs.description: What the visitor wants their day to emphasise, used to shape the plan.

inputs.name: advance confirmation
inputs.description: The visitor's decision to execute the displayed plan.

outputs.primary: A displayed plan of discrete steps, each step's result as it completes, and a final one-day itinerary.
outputs.format: Plan listing followed by progressively revealed step results, with a short educational overview of the planning-agent pattern
outputs.schema_notes: Each plan step carries a description and a kind (research or synthesis); each completed step carries its result and, for research steps, the search queries and result snippets it drew on.

success_criteria: The full plan is visible before any step executes, and no step runs until the visitor advances
Every displayed step produces a visible result, and results appear one by one as they complete
The final itinerary reflects both the city and the stated interests, and draws on the research steps' findings
Each run stays within roughly one planner call plus two to three executor calls, and runs per visit are limited
The overview explains the plan-first approach and explicitly contrasts it with the interleaved reason-act-observe alternative in the gallery
The page states plainly that both limits exist to conserve model capacity and that a planning agent may use any number of steps in general

failure_modes.mode: The planner produces too many steps or steps that cannot be executed
failure_modes.mitigation: Constrain the plan to a small fixed number of steps of the two supported kinds, and reject and regenerate a plan that does not fit

failure_modes.mode: A research step's search returns nothing useful, weakening the itinerary
failure_modes.mitigation: Show the empty or weak observation honestly and let synthesis proceed with what it has, noting the gap

failure_modes.mode: Execution stalls partway, leaving the visitor unsure whether it is still working
failure_modes.mitigation: Show per-step progress continuously and mark a step as failed with an explanation rather than leaving it pending

failure_modes.mode: Visitor exhausts the allowed runs and is confused about which limit was hit
failure_modes.mitigation: Show remaining runs and distinguish this example's per-visit limit from the shared framework-wide cap in the message shown

failure_modes.mode: Ambiguous or fictional city input
failure_modes.mitigation: Let the planner and research steps surface the ambiguity in their visible output rather than failing silently

features.name: Orchestrated_Subagents_Example_App
features.purpose: Demonstrates the orchestrated-subagents pattern: one orchestrating agent reads the visitor's question, chooses exactly two specialists from a fixed roster of four, writes a specific brief for each, dispatches them to run at the same time, and merges their answers into one final response — making fan-out and fan-in visible on screen.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the Orchestrated Subagents example and submits a question or selects a preset; the orchestrator's delegation decision appears, and the visitor then advances to dispatch the two subagents.

inputs.name: visitor question
inputs.description: A free-form question for the orchestrator to route.

inputs.name: preset question choice
inputs.description: A curated question chosen to exercise a particular specialist pairing.

inputs.name: specialist roster
inputs.description: The four fixed specialists — Technical, Financial, Historical and Practical — each knowledge-only with no external tools.

inputs.name: dispatch confirmation
inputs.description: The visitor's decision to dispatch the displayed delegation plan.

outputs.primary: The orchestrator's delegation decision (chosen pair, rationale, and per-specialist brief), two side-by-side subagent tracks with live status and their answers, and a single merged final response.
outputs.format: Delegation summary, then parallel tracks, then merged answer, with a short educational overview and a visible remaining-runs indicator
outputs.schema_notes: Each subagent track carries the specialist name, the brief written for it, its status, and its answer; the final response indicates how the two contributions were combined.

success_criteria: Exactly two specialists are chosen from the roster of four, with a rationale and a distinct brief for each shown before dispatch
The two subagents run at the same time and their independent progress is visible side by side
The final response reflects both subagents' contributions rather than only one
Different preset questions produce different specialist pairings
Each run uses exactly one orchestration call and two subagent calls, and runs per visit are limited to three with a visible remaining-runs indicator

When runs are exhausted, input and the advance action are unavailable with a clear explanation, previous results stay on screen, and the message distinguishes this example's three-run limit from the shared framework-wide daily cap
The overview explains why independent subagents can run in parallel

failure_modes.mode: The orchestrator selects an implausible pairing or fewer/more than two specialists
failure_modes.mitigation: Require exactly two selections from the fixed roster and reject and retry a decision that does not comply

failure_modes.mode: One subagent fails or is refused while the other succeeds
failure_modes.mitigation: Show the failed track's state honestly and merge from what is available, saying plainly that one contribution is missing

failure_modes.mode: The merged answer simply concatenates the two answers, obscuring the fan-in
failure_modes.mitigation: Require the merge to reconcile and attribute the two contributions in a single coherent response

failure_modes.mode: Parallel tracks appear to complete simultaneously so parallelism is not visible
failure_modes.mitigation: Show per-track status changes as they happen rather than only at completion

failure_modes.mode: A visitor's free-form question suits none of the specialists
failure_modes.mitigation: Let the orchestrator state the mismatch in its rationale and still choose the closest pairing

features.name: Multi_Agent_Collaboration_Example_App
features.purpose: Demonstrates peer agents negotiating across a trust boundary rather than workers under one owner: a Buyer agent acting for the visitor runs one competitive procurement round against two rival Seller agents that each hold private constraints, exchange structured messages only with their counterpart, and are judged on deliberately non-comparable terms.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the Multi-Agent Collaboration example, selects a preset procurement scenario and priority weighting, and starts the negotiation round.

inputs.name: preset scenario choice
inputs.description: A pre-tuned procurement scenario whose sellers' private constraints yield genuinely non-comparable bids.

inputs.name: priority weighting
inputs.type: set of ranked or weighted preferences
inputs.description: The visitor's relative emphasis on price, delivery speed, full quantity and warranty length.

inputs.name: seller private positions
inputs.description: Each seller's hidden cost floor, stock level, delivery capability and support capacity, visible to neither the buyer nor the rival seller during the run.

inputs.name: raw exchange view preference
inputs.description: The visitor's choice to view the run as chronological sender-to-recipient message traffic.

outputs.primary: A completed negotiation round showing the request for quotation, two rival bids, the buyer's targeted counter-offers, best-and-final revised bids, and an awarded deal with a rationale weighed against the visitor's priorities — followed by a reveal of every party's previously hidden constraints.
outputs.format: Two parallel seller tracks with live status plus a buyer track, an optional chronological message view, and a short educational overview
outputs.schema_notes: Each agent publishes an inspectable identity summary (name, provider, skills, capabilities); each exchange is a structured task/message/result addressed from one named party to another; the reveal pairs each seller's final position with the constraints that produced it.

success_criteria: Exactly three agents participate and exactly six model calls occur per round, in the stated order, with the request for quotation composed from the preset and priorities without any model call
The two sellers bid without any visibility of each other's messages at either bidding stage, and the chronological message view shows no message ever passing seller to seller
Each agent's published identity summary can be inspected by the visitor
The same scenario can yield a different winner when the visitor changes their priority weighting
The award rationale explicitly weighs the bids against the visitor's stated priorities across the non-comparable axes
The end-of-run reveal explains why each seller held firm or conceded, matching what was observable during the round

The overview states candidly that all three agents ship inside one project under one owner, that the trust boundary is staged for teaching, that this uses the peer-agent interaction model and data shapes without a network transport, what a real deployment would add, and that the pattern's own tier would call this over-engineering for a real system
Runs per hour follow the framework's standard allowance rather than a tightened per-app limit, and the shared hourly and daily caps hold total usage

failure_modes.mode: A seller's response leaks or infers the rival's position, collapsing the trust boundary
failure_modes.mitigation: Enforce message visibility so a peer can only ever receive messages addressed to it, independently of what any instruction asks, and show the message traffic so the property is checkable

failure_modes.mode: Bids come back trivially comparable, so the buyer's judgment looks mechanical
failure_modes.mitigation: Pre-tune each preset's private constraints so the four axes genuinely trade off, and verify that no single bid dominates

failure_modes.mode: A seller's bid or the buyer's award is malformed or incomplete
failure_modes.mitigation: Require each exchange to carry the expected terms, retry a non-conforming reply once, and otherwise present the shortfall candidly

failure_modes.mode: One seller call fails, leaving an uneven negotiation
failure_modes.mitigation: Show that seller's track as failed and let the buyer award on the remaining bid with the shortfall stated

failure_modes.mode: Visitors mistake this staged boundary for a real cross-organisation deployment
failure_modes.mitigation: Place the candid framing note in the overview and repeat it next to the run itself

failure_modes.mode: Six calls per round exhausts shared capacity quickly under traffic
failure_modes.mitigation: Account for the full round against the shared hourly and daily allowances before starting and refuse to start a round that cannot complete

features.name: ReAct_Loop_Example_App
features.purpose: Demonstrates the interleaved reason–act–observe loop in deliberate contrast to the gallery's plan-first planning agent: for a multi-hop question the model thinks, chooses either a search or to answer, reads the observation, and only then decides its next step — with the whole trace filled in live and both success and budget-exhaustion endings shown honestly.

invocation.trigger: A visitor opens the ReAct Loop example, chooses one of five curated multi-hop questions or types their own, and starts the run.

inputs.name: preset question choice
inputs.description: One of five curated multi-hop questions, each requiring at least two chained facts where the later query cannot be written until the earlier result is read, and each containing at least one hop that defeats memorised knowledge because it is time-variable or genuinely obscure.

inputs.name: visitor question
inputs.description: The visitor's own question, run under the same cycle budget.

inputs.name: cycle budget
inputs.description: The fixed ceiling of roughly eight search actions plus one final-answer call per run.

outputs.primary: A live trace of cycles — each showing the model's short thought, the action it chose (the exact query issued, or its decision that it can now answer), and the observation returned — ending in either a final answer card naming the observations it drew on, or a budget-exhausted card presenting the partial trace and naming what remained unresolved.
outputs.format: Progressively filled trace with a live cycle counter and a remaining-runs indicator, preceded by a short educational overview
outputs.schema_notes: Each cycle carries thought, action (query text or answer decision), and observation (result snippets or an explicit empty result); presets store questions only and never stored answers, so time-variable answers come from fresh search on every run.

success_criteria: No plan is shown before the run and the visitor approves nothing mid-run; each next step follows an observation
Each cycle's thought visibly builds on the observation immediately preceding it
The exact query issued and the snippets returned are both shown for every search action
Presets one through three produce at least one run in which every hop's fact demonstrably comes from an observation

The overview explains the loop, distinguishes it from a single decision about whether to search and from a fixed pre-approved plan, and notes that on the two more familiar presets the model may state an early hop from its own knowledge and spend its searches where observation is genuinely needed
A live cycle counter advances during the run so the budget being consumed is visible
Runs end in exactly one of the two stated endings, and a budget-exhausted ending is presented as such rather than as an answer

Runs per visit are limited to two with a visible remaining-runs indicator; once exhausted, input and the start action are unavailable with a clear explanation, previous results remain on screen, and the message distinguishes this example's two-run limit from the shared framework-wide cap
Preset questions remain answerable over time without any maintenance beyond an occasional check that each question still reads sensibly

failure_modes.mode: The model answers from memory without searching, so the trace shows no real observation doing work
failure_modes.mitigation: Curate presets so at least one hop is time-variable or obscure enough to defeat memorised knowledge, and reserve presets one through three as guaranteed fully-observed demonstrations

failure_modes.mode: The loop wanders, repeating near-identical queries until the budget is gone
failure_modes.mitigation: Cap cycles, show the counter so the visitor can anticipate the ending, and present the honest budget-exhausted card naming what remained unresolved

failure_modes.mode: A search returns nothing useful and the model invents an observation
failure_modes.mitigation: Render observations verbatim from the search results so any fabrication is visibly absent from the observation, and treat empty results as explicit observations

failure_modes.mode: A free-form question is unanswerable or single-hop, so the loop is uninteresting or fails
failure_modes.mitigation: Run it under the same budget and end candidly, with the overview noting free-form questions are the likeliest budget-exhausted case

failure_modes.mode: A generous budget makes this the most expensive example and drains shared capacity
failure_modes.mitigation: Apply the gallery's tightest per-visit run limit here and account every search and model call against the shared hourly and daily allowances

failure_modes.mode: A preset becomes stale because its underlying facts change
failure_modes.mitigation: Keep presets as questions only so answers refresh from search on every run

nfr_goals: Every example app follows the same overall layout and navigation, so a visitor who understands one can immediately use the next
Every example app opens with a short educational overview, so a visitor learns the pattern even without running it
Every example makes its inner workings visible — intermediate results, queries issued, observations returned, delegation decisions — rather than only final answers
The gallery is free to visit and requires no sign-up or personal information
Total model and search usage stays within fixed hourly and daily allowances no matter how many visitors arrive, and no visitor can consume a disproportionate share
When any usage limit is reached, the visitor is told plainly which limit it was and any results already produced remain on screen
Static content and plots appear within about a second; runs that involve model work show progress immediately and reveal intermediate results as they complete rather than waiting for the end
Failures — refusals, empty searches, exhausted budgets, unavailable capacity — are always reported candidly and never presented as successful results
New example apps can be added to the gallery without altering existing ones, and appear in the entry-point roster and navigation together
The gallery is usable on common desktop and mobile screen sizes and readable by assistive technologies
